analysis.one_liner: Lets the government strip monopoly protections from brand-name drugs priced far above what other wealthy countries pay.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate in May 2025 with 7 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the health committee, where it has received no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Department to review every brand-name drug's price at least once a year and on petition by any person. If a drug costs more in the U.S. than the median price in Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Japan — or more than is reasonable given its development costs, revenues, and patient population — the government would void its exclusivity and issue open licenses so any company could make a cheaper generic or biosimilar, paying the patent holder a reasonable royalty. Manufacturers would also have to report pricing, research, and advertising spending publicly.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay U.S. retail prices for brand-name drugs, including the roughly half of Americans on employer or individual insurance plans and Medicare beneficiaries who pay coinsurance based on list prices, plus taxpayers who fund Medicare, Medicaid, and employer tax subsidies. Independent generic and biosimilar manufacturers would gain a new pathway to sell approved versions of monopolized drugs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and taxpayers who pay drug prices

how_it_helps.text: A drug whose U.S. price exceeds the median price in Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Japan is automatically deemed 'excessively priced', and the government then voids its exclusivity and licenses anyone to make it [S2][S3].

Companies taking a license must sell the drug below the excessive price and pay the patent holder a reasonable royalty, so the patent holder is still compensated while competition pushes prices down [S2][S3].
The Food and Drug Administration would have to act on generic and biosimilar applications for licensed drugs within 8 months, speeding the arrival of cheaper versions [S2][S3].
Any person could petition the government for an excessive-price determination, and all determinations, petitions, and manufacturer price data would go into a public database [S2][S3].

Manufacturers that raise a drug's price after an excessive-price determination — before a generic maker starts production — could be sued by the government to recover all revenue from the increase [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose government-granted monopolies would end on drugs judged excessively priced, cutting the monopoly profits that flow to their shareholders. Honest supporters would also acknowledge a possible cost in slower development of future drugs if expected returns shrink.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug manufacturers and their investors

drawbacks.text: Cutting the monopoly returns that finance pharmaceutical research could reduce investment in new drugs over time; the bill tries to blunt this by guaranteeing a royalty to the patent holder, but a guaranteed royalty on an open license is worth less than an exclusivity period, and critics of international reference pricing have argued it shifts research decisions toward drugs that can command U.S. prices [S3].

The bill puts enormous discretion in the hands of the HHS Secretary: the alternative 'reasonable price' test weighs factors like 'value to patients' and 'other factors the Secretary determines appropriate', so determinations could vary sharply by administration and would almost certainly be litigated for years [S3].

Manufacturers face a new annual reporting regime covering prices, revenues, research spending by trial, and advertising, with civil penalties of 0.5% to 1% of a drug's gross revenues per day of noncompliance — a compliance burden that falls on the industry but whose costs could be passed through [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the upside is direct and large: government monopoly protections are the main reason U.S. brand-name drugs sell for several times what the same drugs cost in other wealthy countries, and this bill targets exactly that gap while still paying patent holders a royalty. The main honest cost is the possibility of slower new-drug development, a tradeoff the bill addresses only partially through its royalty scheme, and the likelihood of prolonged litigation and administrative disputes over what counts as 'reasonable'.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has taken no further action on it; the Congress is still in session, so it is not formally dead but has gone nowhere.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on May 20, 2025, with six Democratic cosponsors listed on the bill text (Blumenthal, Booker, Merkley, Murphy, Welch, and Warren) [S1][S3].

It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, vote, or discharge petition since [S5].
No Republican senators cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off so far: with the bill sitting untouched in committee, U.S. monopoly prices continue unchanged, and no foreign-reference-pricing regime has been created.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator (I-VT), bill sponsor and Ranking Member of the Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Prescription Drug Price Relief Act of 2025 and recruited Senate cosponsors.

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal, Cory Booker, Jeff Merkley, Chris Murphy, Peter Welch, and Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill at introduction.

against.name: HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Chairman Bill Cassidy (R-LA) and the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee, which holds jurisdiction over the bill, has held no hearing or markup and has not reported it to the floor in the months since referral.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug manufacturers and their trade groups (e.g. PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: The industry has long campaigned against international reference pricing and government intervention in drug pricing, and has made protecting patent exclusivity a core lobbying priority.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat or independent who caucuses with Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in a committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: Their government-granted monopolies — the legal barrier that lets U.S. brand-name drugs sell for several times the price in peer countries — would be voided on any drug the Secretary deems excessively priced, with only a royalty left. Their interest in keeping the status quo runs directly against patients paying U.S. list prices.

Open, non-exclusive licenses and an 8-month expedited FDA review would create a steady pipeline of new generic and biosimilar markets they can enter. Their gain is the patient's savings: they only profit if they sell below the excessive price.

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic cosponsors, no hearing or markup after referral, and a Republican-chaired committee controlling the schedule, the most likely path is that the bill sits in committee for the rest of the 119th Congress without a vote. Comparable drug-pricing bills have advanced only when attached to larger must-pass packages; nothing in the record suggests that here.
